en: An open insult; to insult intentionally
hook: AFFRONT: an insult right to your FRONT, to your face.
story: Affront. An open insult; as a verb, to insult intentionally. At his daughter's wedding, Hank had welcomed every guest personally. Then one rich relative arrived late, looked at the food, and announced loudly that he would eat at a hotel instead. The guests went silent, and Hank's face burned. It was an affront to his whole family, in front of everyone. Affront comes from the Latin for to the face, so an affront is an insult thrown right in your face. So, what word names an open insult delivered on purpose? ... Affront.

gre.s: The ambassador regarded the decision to seat him behind junior officials as a deliberate ____, a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology.
gre.clue: a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology

example: Being left off the guest list for her cousin's wedding felt like an affront to Nasrin, who had helped plan every detail of the engagement.

en: Telling a story whose characters and events stand for deeper ideas
hook: ALLEGORICAL: ALL the story is a symbol for something else.
story: Allegorical. Telling a story whose characters and events stand for deeper ideas. In Rita's literature class, the teacher read from George Orwell's Animal Farm, where pigs take over a farm and slowly become as cruel as the humans they replaced. At first Rita thought it was just a story about animals. Then she [gasp] realised the pigs stood for real rulers. The novel was allegorical. The root allo means other in Greek, so an allegorical story speaks of one thing while meaning another. So, what word describes a story whose characters stand for deeper ideas? ... Allegorical.

gre.s: Readers who take the fable literally miss its point; its talking animals are plainly ____, each standing for a faction in the political struggles of the author's day.
gre.clue: each standing for a faction

example: Visitors to the gallery debated whether the painter's sinking boat was allegorical or just a memory of a real ferry accident.

en: Open and willing to be persuaded or to cooperate
hook: AMENABLE: says 'AMEN' readily, agreeing to your suggestion.
story: Amenable. Open and willing to be persuaded or to cooperate. Ray expected a long fight when he told his parents he wanted to study film instead of engineering. He prepared charts, examples and a whole speech. But his father listened quietly, asked two questions, and said yes. Ray [laugh] could not believe how amenable he was. His mother, it turned out, had been amenable for months. Amenable comes from the old French for to lead, so an amenable person is easy to lead toward agreement. So, what word describes someone open to persuasion? ... Amenable.

gre.s: Although the director was initially stubborn about the ending, she proved ____ to suggestions once the test audiences reacted poorly.
gre.clue: Although the director was initially stubborn

example: The landlord proved amenable to a lower rent once Tania offered to repaint the flat herself.

en: Cleverly skilled, often at tricking or manipulating others
hook: ARTFUL: full of the ART of tricks — the opposite of artless.
story: Artful. Cleverly skilled, often at tricking or manipulating others. In a busy street market, a seller held up a cheap watch and spun such a charming story about its Swiss origins that a crowd gathered around him. He flattered each buyer, lowered the price twice, and sold ten watches in ten minutes. Ted [chuckle] had to admire the artful performance, though he kept his wallet in his pocket. Artful means full of the art of tricks, and its opposite, artless, means simple and honest. So, what word describes someone cleverly skilled at manipulating others? ... Artful.

gre.s: The senator's ____ evasions impressed even her opponents: she could sidestep a damaging question so smoothly that reporters rarely noticed it had gone unanswered.
gre.clue: so smoothly that reporters rarely noticed it had gone unanswered

example: With an artful bit of flattery, the young salesman persuaded my grandmother to buy two pressure cookers she never needed.

en: So common and unoriginal that it is boring
hook: BANAL: as boring as a BANANA, which you've eaten a thousand times.
story: Banal. So common and unoriginal that it is boring. At her cousin's wedding, Nadia listened to six speeches in a row. Each one said the same things: two hearts became one, love is a journey, and marriage is a beautiful garden. By the fourth speech, even the groom [sigh] was staring at the ceiling. The words were kind, but completely banal. Long ago in France, banal described things shared by a whole village, like a common oven, so banal ideas are common to all. So, what word describes words so ordinary that they are dull? ... Banal.

gre.s: Though the speech was praised for its delivery, its content was ____, a string of platitudes the audience had heard countless times.
gre.clue: a string of platitudes the audience had heard countless times

example: The song's lyrics were so banal, rhyming 'heart' with 'apart' in every verse, that the judges eliminated it in the first round.

en: To talk about someone or something as if they hardly matter
hook: BE-LITTLE: make it LITTLE.
story: Belittle. To talk about someone or something as if they hardly matter. When Stella told her brothers that she had won a national science prize, the eldest smirked and said that school prizes were easy to win. Her face fell. Their grandmother put down her knitting and told him sharply never to belittle his sister again. Then she asked Stella to explain the project twice, slowly, with pride. To belittle is to make something little, to shrink it with words. So, what verb means to make someone's achievement seem unimportant? ... Belittle.

gre.s: Insecure about his own modest achievements, the manager tended to ____ the accomplishments of his subordinates, dismissing even their major successes as mere luck.
gre.clue: dismissing even their major successes as mere luck

example: A good coach never belittles a nervous swimmer after a false start, because shame rarely makes anyone faster.

en: Loud, lively, and full of high spirits, sometimes unruly
hook: BOISTEROUS: BOYS-terous, a room full of loud, playful boys.
story: Boisterous. Loud, lively, and full of high spirits, sometimes unruly. On the last school day before the holidays, class seven in a small-town school went wild. Boys drummed on desks, girls sang film songs, and someone threw paper planes out of the window. The teacher tried to look stern, but [laugh] ended up laughing too. It was a boisterous, happy afternoon. Hear boys inside boisterous, and picture a classroom of loud, playful children. So, what word describes a crowd that is noisy, lively and a little wild? ... Boisterous.

gre.s: The usually ____ classroom fell completely silent when the principal walked in unannounced.
gre.clue: fell completely silent

example: The boisterous cousins turned the wedding's quiet garden into a cricket pitch until an aunt confiscated the ball.

en: Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters
hook: CANNY: like a CAN-do person who's never fooled.
story: Canny. Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters. Rhoda sells vegetables at the big wholesale market. She buys tomatoes in the early hours when prices are low, watches the weather on her phone, and never lets anyone cheat her on the scale. Before a big storm, she stocked up on potatoes and sold them at a fair profit when supplies ran short. She is a canny trader. Canny comes from can, in its old sense of knowing how, so a canny person knows how to win. So, what word describes someone shrewd and careful with money? ... Canny.

gre.s: A ____ negotiator, she waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer, securing the property far below its asking price.
gre.clue: waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer

example: Canny shoppers at New Market know to walk away once while bargaining, since the seller usually calls them back with a lower price.

en: Frustration mixed with embarrassment after a failure or humiliation
hook: CHAGRIN: you wanted to GRIN, but SHAME (cha) took over.
story: Chagrin. Frustration mixed with embarrassment after a failure or humiliation. Nick told everyone in his office that he would surely win the company chess tournament. He even cleared a shelf for the trophy. In the first round, a quiet new trainee beat him in twelve moves, and much to his chagrin, the whole office was watching. Nick [sigh] smiled weakly and shook her hand. Chagrin is the French word for sorrow; in English, it is the sour feeling of being let down and embarrassed together. So, what word names the embarrassed frustration you feel after a public failure? ... Chagrin.

gre.s: Much to the general's ____, the battle he had boasted would last a single afternoon dragged on for months, exposing his strategy as hopelessly naive.
gre.clue: he had boasted would last a single afternoon

example: To the chef's chagrin, the visiting food critic sent back the biryani because the rice was undercooked.

en: An expert judge in matters of taste, especially art, food, or drink
hook: CONNOISSEUR: 'connaître' is French for 'to know'. One who really knows.
story: Connoisseur. An expert judge in matters of taste, especially art, food, or drink. Mindy's grandfather has tasted tea for fifty years. He can sip a cup and tell you which garden it came from, whether it was picked in the first flush of spring, and how long it was rolled. Tea companies send him samples from all over the country. He is a true connoisseur. Connoisseur comes from the old French for to know, so a connoisseur is someone who really knows. So, what word names an expert in matters of taste? ... Connoisseur.

gre.s: Only a true ____ of early jazz could distinguish the original recordings from the expert imitations that flooded the market in the 1950s.
gre.clue: could distinguish the original recordings from the expert imitations

example: A connoisseur of handloom saris, Shahana can tell a genuine Jamdani from a machine copy by running a fingertip over the weave.

en: Behavior that is polite, proper, and appropriate to the situation
hook: DECORUM is related to DECORATE: decent, proper presentation.
story: Decorum. Behaviour that is polite, proper, and appropriate to the situation. At the national war memorial on Victory Day, thousands of people walked in silence and laid flowers at the base of the tall monument. Even small children held their parents' hands and kept quiet. When a young man started playing loud music on his phone, an old man gently touched his shoulder, and he switched it off. The day called for decorum. Decorum shares a root with decorate, meaning fitting and proper. So, what word names proper, dignified behaviour suited to the occasion? ... Decorum.

gre.s: The senator was censured for violating the chamber's ____, having shouted insults at a colleague during a solemn debate.
gre.clue: having shouted insults at a colleague

example: The memorial service was conducted with quiet decorum until a phone with a loud ringtone went off in the front row.

en: Quick and skillful, especially with the hands
hook: DEFT sounds like the opposite of DAFT: not stupid, but skilled.
story: Deft. Quick and skillful, especially with the hands. Every evening outside an old church in the old city, an old man named Bert makes flatbread. With a few deft movements he stretches the dough, folds it into layers, slaps it onto the hot pan, and flips it with his bare fingers. Passers-by stop to film him, amazed. His hands are deft after forty years of practice. Deft sounds like the opposite of daft: daft means foolish, but deft means skilled. So, what word describes hands that move quickly and skilfully? ... Deft.

gre.s: The diplomat's ____ handling of the dispute, defusing it with a single well-chosen compromise, earned praise from both sides.
gre.clue: defusing it with a single well-chosen compromise

example: With a few deft strokes of the brush, the rickshaw painter added a tiger to the back panel in under five minutes.

en: Deep moral rottenness; extreme wickedness
hook: DEPRAVITY: DEPRIVED of all goodness.
story: Depravity. Deep moral rottenness; extreme wickedness. A city court heard how a gang had kidnapped children from railway stations and forced them to beg on the streets, keeping every coin for themselves. Even the experienced judge paused while reading the evidence. He called the crime an act of shocking depravity, and the whole courtroom was silent. The root pravus is Latin for crooked, so depravity is a soul bent completely out of shape. So, what word names extreme moral wickedness? ... Depravity.

gre.s: The prosecutor described the crimes as acts of shocking ____, committed not out of desperation but out of sheer delight in the suffering of others.
gre.clue: sheer delight in the suffering of others

example: The novel traces a gifted student's slow slide into depravity, from small lies to cheating and finally to blackmail.

en: Excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws
hook: DRACONIAN: from DRACO, an ancient Greek lawmaker who gave the death penalty for small crimes.
story: Draconian. Excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws. In Simon's dorm, a new warden announced rules that shocked everyone: gates locked at seven, no phones after nine, and a fine of fifty dollars for one late return. Students who missed the gate by a minute had to sleep outside. The rules were so draconian that parents complained, and the draconian rules were relaxed within a month. The word comes from Draco, a lawmaker in ancient Athens whose laws gave the death penalty even for small crimes. So, what word describes rules that are excessively harsh? ... Draconian.

gre.s: Critics condemned the law as ____, pointing out that it imposed ten year prison sentences for offenses as trivial as littering.
gre.clue: ten year prison sentences for offenses as trivial as littering

example: The company's draconian attendance policy docked a full day's pay from any worker who arrived even five minutes late.

en: To invent something false in order to deceive; to construct
hook: FABRICATE: FABRIC of lies, stitched together.
story: Fabricate. To invent something false in order to deceive; also, to construct. When Robbie missed three weeks of classes, he fabricated a story about a sick uncle in another town and even forged a medical letter. But his teacher called the uncle, who answered the phone cheerfully from a cricket ground. [chuckle] Robbie's fabricated story fell apart. Fabricate shares a root with fabric, from the Latin for making, so to fabricate a lie is to stitch it together like cloth. So, what verb means to invent a false story to deceive? ... Fabricate.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed after editors discovered that she had chosen to ____ several quotations, attributing to real officials words they had never spoken.
gre.clue: attributing to real officials words they had never spoken

example: Investigators found that the lab had fabricated data for at least four published studies, and the journal retracted all of them.

en: Unfortunate; unlucky
hook: HAP-LESS: without HAPpiness or luck (hap = luck).
story: Hapless. Unfortunate; unlucky. On the morning of his job interview, hapless Steve missed his bus, got splashed by a passing car, and stepped into a puddle in his new shoes. At the office, the lift was broken, so he climbed nine floors. He reached the room [sigh] dripping and breathless, only to learn the interview had been moved to the next day. Hap is an old word for luck, as in happen and perhaps, so hapless means without luck. So, what word describes someone unlucky again and again? ... Hapless.

gre.s: The ____ explorer seemed cursed: his ship sank, his supplies were stolen, and when he finally reached the coast, he found it already claimed by a rival.
gre.clue: seemed cursed

example: The hapless goalkeeper slipped on the wet grass twice in the same match, gifting the visitors both of their goals.

en: Not allowing fluid to pass through; unaffected by
hook: IMPERVIOUS: nothing gets through, waterproof to water or criticism.
story: Impervious. Not allowing fluid to pass through; also, unaffected by something. Before the monsoon, Kent's father coated the tin roof with a thick layer of tar so it would be impervious to rain. That season, not a single drop leaked. Kent's grandmother was impervious in a different way: no matter how loudly the grandchildren argued, she kept peacefully shelling peas. Per means through and via means way, so impervious means with no way through. So, what word describes something that nothing can get through or affect? ... Impervious.

gre.s: So convinced was the director of her own vision that she seemed ____ to criticism, continuing to film exactly as she had planned despite the producers' increasingly anxious notes.
gre.clue: continuing to film exactly as she had planned

example: Seemingly impervious to the heat, the old farmer kept planting seedlings through the noon sun while his sons rested in the shade.

en: Angry at something unjust
hook: INDIGNANT: your DIGNITY was insulted.
story: Indignant. Angry at something unjust. Irene had waited three hours in the heat in a long queue at the passport office. Then a man in sunglasses walked straight to the front and handed his papers to a clerk he knew. The whole queue grew indignant. Irene spoke up politely but firmly, and the clerk sent the man to the back. Indignant is linked to dignity: when something unfair insults your dignity, you become indignant. So, what word describes anger at unfair treatment? ... Indignant.

gre.s: Accused of a theft she had not committed, the housekeeper was not frightened but ____, demanding an apology from the family that had wrongly suspected her.
gre.clue: a theft she had not committed

example: Passengers grew indignant when the bus company doubled its fares overnight, without any notice, just before Eid.

en: The lowest point
hook: NADIR: the opposite of zenith, the bottom of everything.
story: Nadir. The lowest point. After failing an exam and losing his part-time job in the same week, Tom sat alone on the steps of the old university hall, feeling that his life had reached its nadir. Then his old teacher passed by, sat down beside him, and offered to tutor him for free. Two years later, Tom teaches others. That week was his nadir, but it was also where he turned around. Nadir is the opposite of zenith, the highest point in the sky. So, what word names the lowest point of something? ... Nadir.

gre.s: The team's season reached its ____ in March, when a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place; only then did its slow recovery begin.
gre.clue: a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place

example: Relations between the two sisters hit their nadir when they argued over their mother's house and stopped speaking for a year.

en: Small or meager; worthless
hook: PALTRY: like a PALTRY chicken — PALLID and puny.
story: Paltry. Small or meager; worthless. After working twelve hours a day for a month at a roadside hotel, young Billy was handed his salary: a paltry one hundred dollars. The owner said food and a bench to sleep on were the rest of his pay. Billy's cousin, a lawyer, helped him find a fairer job in a bakery. Paltry once meant made of rags and rubbish, so a paltry sum is hardly worth anything. So, what word describes an amount that is shamefully small? ... Paltry.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the raise it offered its workers was ____, amounting to less than the price of a cup of tea per day.
gre.clue: amounting to less than the price of a cup of tea per day

example: After three months of selling handmade candles, Rumana had earned a paltry five hundred taka, barely enough to cover the wax.

en: Seemingly contradictory but possibly true
hook: PARADOX: two contradictory things that are both true.
story: Paradoxical. Seemingly contradictory but possibly true. Shelly's grandfather says something that sounds strange: the more he gives away, the richer he feels. He shares his mangoes with the whole lane, and every season the neighbours bring back rice cakes, fish and friendship. It sounds paradoxical, giving more to have more, yet his life proves it true. Para means beyond and dox means opinion, so a paradoxical idea goes beyond what we expect to believe. So, what word describes a statement that seems to contradict itself but may be true? ... Paradoxical.

gre.s: It may seem ____ that adding new roads can worsen traffic, yet studies show that extra lanes often attract so many new drivers that congestion increases.
gre.clue: yet studies show

example: It seems paradoxical that the busiest people often reply to emails fastest, yet they usually have the most practiced routines.

en: Slowly and quietly causing serious harm or damage
hook: PERNICIOUS: slowly PERISHING you.
story: Pernicious. Slowly and quietly causing serious harm or damage. For years, Ross's family drank from a tube well whose water tasted perfectly fresh. Nobody knew that arsenic was seeping into it from deep underground. Only when spots appeared on his father's skin did a health worker test the well. The poison had been pernicious, harming them silently for years. Pernicious comes from the Latin for destruction, and pernicious things destroy quietly. So, what word describes harm that works slowly and silently? ... Pernicious.

gre.s: The rumors were all the more ____ for being subtle: no single falsehood seemed serious, yet together they slowly destroyed public trust in the institution.
gre.clue: yet together they slowly destroyed public trust

example: Constant comparison on social media can have a pernicious effect on teenagers, eroding their confidence a little each day.

en: Developing skills or maturity much earlier than is usual
hook: PRE-COCIOUS: PRE-COOKED early, ripe too soon.
story: Precocious. Developing skills or maturity much earlier than is usual. At four, Theo could read the newspaper aloud. At seven, he was solving his elder sister's class nine maths problems, while she [laugh] pretended not to notice. His teachers called him the most precocious child they had ever met. Precocious comes from the Latin for cooked or ripened early, so a precocious child is like fruit that ripens before its season. So, what word describes a child who develops unusually early? ... Precocious.

gre.s: Remarkably ____, the boy was reading novels at three and solving algebra problems at six, years before most of his peers could do either.
gre.clue: years before most of his peers could do either

example: A precocious violinist, Arnob joined the city orchestra at eleven and played his first solo concert at Shilpakala Academy a year later.

en: High-pitched and piercing; loud and forceful in criticism
hook: SHRILL: like a SHRIEKING whistle.
story: Shrill. High-pitched and piercing; also, loud and forceful in criticism. Every morning at six, the shrill whistle of a factory near town cut through the fog, and Kathy's whole neighbourhood woke at once. Kathy would pull the pillow over her head. Later, when the factory tried to run its machines all night, the residents' protests became just as shrill, and their complaints filled the local papers for a week. Shrill sounds like shriek, and both pierce your ears. So, what word describes a sound so high and sharp that it hurts the ears? ... Shrill.

gre.s: The opposition's attacks grew increasingly ____, so loud and relentless that even sympathetic voters began to dismiss them as hysteria rather than reasoned argument.
gre.clue: so loud and relentless

example: The kettle's shrill whistle woke the whole household before dawn, ending any hope Raju had of sleeping late.

en: To calm down or ease off after being intense or severe
hook: SUB-SIDE: sinking down (sub) to the side.
story: Subside. To calm down or ease off after being intense or severe. For three days the floodwater stood waist-deep in the streets of the town. On the fourth morning, Nina saw a line of mud on the wall, a hand's width above the water. The flood was beginning to subside. By the end of the week, as the water subsided, people started sweeping out their homes. Sub means down and side comes from the Latin for settle, so to subside is to sink down and settle. So, what verb means to ease off after being intense? ... Subside.

gre.s: The villagers camped on the embankment for three days, waiting for the floodwaters to ____ so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes.
gre.clue: so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes

example: Once the fever began to subside, the doctor allowed Mitu to eat a little rice and lentil soup.

en: Bending and moving easily; flexible
hook: SUPPLE: as soft and flexible as SUPPLE leather.
story: Supple. Bending and moving easily; flexible. At sixty-five, Shirley still practises yoga on her rooftop every dawn. She bends forward until her palms touch the floor, while her twenty-year-old grandson [chuckle] groans halfway down. Her body is as supple as a bamboo stem in the wind. The word can also describe soft leather, or a mind that bends easily. Think of young bamboo: supple things bend without breaking. So, what word describes a body that bends easily and gracefully? ... Supple.

gre.s: Years of daily yoga had kept the old man remarkably ____: at eighty, he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes.
gre.clue: he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes

example: Soaked overnight in water, dry cane becomes supple enough for basket weavers in Sylhet to bend it into tight circles.

en: An extended, furious outburst that attacks someone or something
hook: TIRADE: so long it TIRES everyone out.
story: Tirade. An extended, furious outburst that attacks someone or something. When the electricity went out for the fifth time one summer evening, Fran's uncle stood on the balcony and launched into a tirade against the power company, the government, the weather and even the mosquitoes. Fran [sigh] waited. He went on for twenty minutes. Then the lights came back, and he [laugh] quietly sat down to watch the news. Picture a tirade so long it tires everyone out, though the word really comes from an Italian word for a volley of shots. So, what word names a long, angry outburst? ... Tirade.

gre.s: Instead of offering constructive feedback, the critic launched into a furious ____ against the novel, denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages.
gre.clue: denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages

example: The taxi driver's tirade against the city's potholes lasted the entire forty-minute ride from Uttara to Motijheel.

en: An act that violates a rule, law, or moral code
hook: TRANS-GRESS: stepping ACROSS (trans) the line.
story: Transgression. An act that violates a rule, law, or moral code. In Leon's village, the elders had one firm rule: nobody fishes in the pond during the spawning months. One night a young man cast his net anyway, and by morning everyone knew. The elders did not shout; they asked him to restock the pond with young fish himself. He never repeated his transgression. Trans means across and gress means step, so a transgression is stepping across a line you should not cross. So, what word names an act that breaks a rule or moral code? ... Transgression.

gre.s: The senator's minor ____, a forgotten parking fine, was seized upon by opponents eager to portray him as contemptuous of the law.
gre.clue: a forgotten parking fine

example: Under the boarding school's strict code, even reading a novel after lights-out counted as a serious transgression.

en: Hidden beyond what is obvious, usually a selfish motive
hook: ULTERIOR: the motive lies ULTERIOR, further beyond.
story: Ulterior. Hidden beyond what is obvious, usually a selfish motive. A new neighbour suddenly became very friendly with Summer's family, bringing sweets every Friday and praising her father's garden. Then, after a month, he asked her father to sign as guarantor for a large bank loan. Now the family understood. His kindness had an ulterior motive. Ulterior comes from the Latin for further or beyond, so an ulterior motive lies beyond what you can see. So, what word describes a hidden, selfish motive? ... Ulterior.

gre.s: Though the billionaire insisted that his donation was purely charitable, skeptics suspected that he had ____ motives, noting that it was announced just before his trial began.
gre.clue: announced just before his trial began

example: Rana's sudden offer to wash his sister's car made her wonder what ulterior purpose lay behind such unusual kindness.

en: Extremely damaging or infectious; full of bitter hatred
hook: VIRULENT: like a VIRUS, spreading poison.
story: Virulent. Extremely damaging or infectious; also, full of bitter hatred. When a virulent strain of bird flu reached a poultry farm, it spread through the sheds in days, and the farmer, Jerry, lost thousands of chickens. That same week, a virulent online campaign blamed his family, though they had done nothing wrong. Virulent comes from the Latin virus, meaning poison, so virulent things spread like poison, whether a disease or hatred. So, what word describes something extremely harmful and fast-spreading, or bitterly hostile? ... Virulent.

gre.s: The pamphlet's ____ attacks on the minority community, full of hateful slurs, led to its immediate ban.
gre.clue: full of hateful slurs

example: Public health officers in Chattogram tracked a virulent strain of cholera that spread through three neighborhoods within a week.
